metaTitle: Sugar Ants: Types and How to Get Rid of Them
metaDescription: Sugar ants are not one species. In the US the name is used for several small ants. How to tell which you have and get rid of them with bait, not spray.
h1: Sugar Ants: What They Really Are and How to Get Rid of Them
dek: Sugar ant is a nickname, not a species. Here is how to work out which small ant is trailing to your counter, why it came indoors, and the bait-first plan university entomologists recommend for getting rid of it.
excerpt: Sugar ants are a nickname for several small sweet-feeding ants, not one species. How to tell which one you have and the bait-first steps that get rid of them.

quickAnswer.lead: **Sugar ants are not one species: in the US the name is a nickname for small ants that trail to sweets, and extension publications attach it to at least three, the odorous house ant, the pavement ant and the pharaoh ant.** To get rid of them, use a slow-acting bait and skip the spray, which [University of California pest management guidance](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/ants/) says will not stop more ants from coming indoors.
bullets: The five small ants covered here run from about 1/16 inch (pharaoh and little black ants) to 3/16 inch (the University of California's figure for pavement ants).
An odorous house ant, about 1/8 inch long and dark brown to black, gives off a strong odor likened to coconut or pine when it is crushed.
With bait, the University of California says to expect 5 to 10 days before you see fewer ants and several weeks or more for full control.
Spraying kills only the foragers you can see, which the University of Kentucky describes as a small portion of a colony that typically holds thousands more.
The ant actually named the sugar ant, the banded sugar ant, is a species native to Australia that grows to about 3/16 to 5/8 inch (5 to 15 mm).

body.text: What are sugar ants?

Sugar ants are not a species. In the United States the name is a household nickname for small ants found trailing to something sweet, and different publications attach it to different ants. [A Pacific Northwest school pest management newsletter on sugar ants](https://s3.wp.wsu.edu/uploads/sites/415/2014/12/PNW_PPSugarAnts.pdf), written by Washington State University's Urban IPM Program, says the region's most common kitchen invaders, pavement ants and odorous house ants, are sometimes called sugar ants because of their attraction to sweet foods.

Other university sources use the name for a single species. [A Pacific Northwest Extension guide to ant management](https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/pnw-761-integrated-pest-management-ants-schools), published by Oregon State University with Washington State University and the University of Idaho, lists sugar ant as another name for the odorous house ant, alongside stink ant and coconut ant. [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's guide to household ant pests](https://extensionentomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Ants_household_B6183.pdf) gives the same nickname to the pharaoh ant, which belongs to a different genus and, unlike the other two, usually nests indoors.

That makes at least three species under one name in university sources alone: the odorous house ant, the pavement ant and the pharaoh ant. Two more small ants that go for sweets indoors, the Argentine ant and the little black ant, fit the same description, so this page covers all five. Which one you have depends partly on where you live. The University of California calls the Argentine ant the most common ant in and around homes and gardens in California, Texas A&M says the pharaoh ant is the ant most often seen indoors in Texas, and [the University of Kentucky's ant control guide](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef619) describes the odorous house ant as the most common and difficult ant to control in Kentucky and much of the Midwest.

Nicknames like this describe what an ant is doing, not what it is, in the same way that [zombie ants are ordinary ants infected by a fungus](/blog/zombie-ants) and not a species of their own. All five sugar ant candidates share the colony habits described in [the complete guide to ants in and around US homes](/learn/ants), but they differ enough in nesting and diet that the first job is to work out which one is on your counter.
Is there a real sugar ant?

Yes, but it lives in Australia. The banded sugar ant, *Camponotus consobrinus*, is a native Australian species that [a Queensland Department of Education fact sheet](https://tooheyforesteec.eq.edu.au/support-and-resources/teacher-resources/banded-sugar-ant) describes as 5 to 15 mm long (about 3/16 to 5/8 inch), with a black head, an orange thorax and legs, and usually an orange band across a mostly black abdomen. Its workers are active at night, and its range runs from the Atherton Tablelands in Queensland down to Tasmania. None of the US extension sources used for this page lists it as a household ant, so a sugar ant in an American kitchen is one of the smaller species below.
How do you tell which sugar ant you have?

Size, color and the smell of a crushed worker separate most of them. Collect a few workers (Texas A&M suggests a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol), look at them with a magnifier or a zoomed-in phone camera, and compare them with the table. The measurements and diets come mainly from [the University of California's Pest Notes on ants](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/ants/).

body.text: Texas A&M describes the little black ant as a slow-moving, small, shiny black ant about 1/16 inch long. Its workers prey on insects and feed on honeydew, and the foods it prefers indoors are grease, sweets, meats, fruits and vegetables. Sources differ slightly on the pavement ant: the University of California lists it at 3/16 inch, the Pacific Northwest guide measures workers at 2.5 to 3 mm (roughly 1/10 to 1/8 inch), and the Washington State newsletter gives about 1/16 to 1/8 inch for pavement ant and odorous house ant workers alike.

body.text: Three quick checks

items: **Crush one and smell it.** An odorous house ant gives off a strong odor that the Pacific Northwest guide says can resemble coconut, blue cheese, rancid butter or pine cleaner; the University of Kentucky describes it as rotten coconut or pine.
**Check the color.** A yellow, honey-colored or light tan ant about 1/16 inch long points to the pharaoh ant, and a shiny black ant of the same size points to the little black ant.

**Look at the waist and the nest.** Kentucky says a pavement ant shows two obvious nodes between thorax and abdomen plus fine grooves on its head and thorax, and is the more likely of the two to push soil out from under paved surfaces. An odorous house ant has no noticeable node; the Pacific Northwest guide explains that its single node lies flat and hidden against the abdomen.

body.text: If your ants do not match any row, [the identification key for very small house ants](/blog/tiny-ants) adds thief ants, ghost ants and other look-alikes, and [the guide to black ants around the home](/blog/black-ants) separates the small dark species from carpenter ants.
Why does the species matter?

It matters because the species decides which bait gets eaten. The University of California lists sweets first for odorous house ants and Argentine ants, sweets, proteins and grease for pavement ants, and fats and proteins ahead of sweets for pharaoh ants. It adds that pharaoh ants and thief ants prefer protein or greasy baits year-round, while Argentine ants take sweet baits all year and protein baits mainly in spring. A sugar-based bait that suits odorous house ants may therefore sit untouched in front of pharaoh ants. There is more on [what each household ant eats and how the diet shifts by season](/blog/what-do-ants-eat) in a separate guide.
Why do sugar ants come into the house?

They come in for food, water and shelter. The University of California says ants enter buildings seeking food and water, warmth and shelter, or refuge from hot, dry weather or flooding, and that once inside, household ants feed on sugar, syrup, honey, fruit juice, fats and meat. A sticky jar is an attraction, but so are grease, pet food and a leaky faucet.

Often the nest is still outside. The Washington State newsletter says ants sometimes establish colonies indoors but more commonly nest outside the building and come in to search for food. Kentucky says odorous house ants commonly nest outdoors under mulch, stones, pavement, woodpiles, flower pots and siding and forage indoors for food and moisture, though their nests also turn up inside wall cavities, appliances and potted plants. The Pacific Northwest guide adds that indoor nests sit in wall and floor voids or crawl spaces near warm, moist areas close to food and water, and that indoor colonies stay active all year.

Pharaoh ants are the exception. They are the only species that Texas A&M's table of common house-infesting ants lists as usually nesting indoors, and the same publication names light sockets, potted plants, wall voids and attics among their nest sites, with a liking for warm places close to water.

Outdoors, the draw is often honeydew, the sweet liquid produced by aphids, soft scales and mealybugs. The University of California notes that ants tend and protect these insects, and it advises managing sweet food sources next to the house, such as aphid-infested bushes and ripe fruit on trees.

What you see is a fraction of what is there. Kentucky's guide points out that the ants foraging across a counter are only a small portion of a colony, with thousands more, including one or more egg-laying queens, hidden in the nest. Odorous house ant supercolonies close to human habitation can hold tens or even hundreds of thousands of workers with multiple egg-laying queens, according to the Pacific Northwest guide, and Texas A&M puts a pharaoh ant colony at anywhere from one to several hundred queens. That is why control is aimed at the nest and not at the trail.
How do you get rid of sugar ants?

Bait the trail, leave the ants alone while they feed, remove what attracted them, then seal the gap they used. These are the steps university extension programs describe, and baiting works because workers carry a slow-acting bait back to the nest, where the University of California says it is passed to other workers, larvae and queens. Read the label on any bait you use and follow it.

items: **Find the trail and the entry point.** Follow the line of ants back to the crack, window frame or pipe gap they are using. If the trail is hard to see, Kentucky suggests putting a small dab of honey or jelly on an index card where ants have been seen; after feeding, they head back toward the nest.

**Set bait beside the trail.** Kentucky's advice is to place bait next to wherever ants are seen, preferably beside their trails. The University of California prefers stations outdoors, near nests and along the edges ants travel, and reserves indoor baiting for a serious infestation where you cannot find the entry point. Either way, keep stations where pets and small children cannot reach them; [the guide to ants in the kitchen](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-in-the-kitchen) covers placement around counters and sinks.

**Match the bait to the ant.** Kentucky recommends syrupy, sweet baits for odorous house ants, and the University of California says sweet baits attract Argentine ants all year. For pale pharaoh ants, offer a protein or grease-based bait as well. The University of California's test is simple: put out a small amount of each kind and watch which one the ants choose.

**Let them feed.** Expect more ants at the bait at first. Kentucky says that surge means the bait is being carried home and that activity usually subsides in a few days. Do not spray the ants, and do not use insecticides or cleaning products around the bait.
**Take away food and water.** Store food in clean, sealed containers, wipe up crumbs, grease and spills, take out the garbage often, do not leave pet food sitting out, and fix leaky faucets.

**Clean up the trails.** Sponge or mop them with soapy water, which the University of California says removes the ants' scent trail, especially when the entry points are cleaned thoroughly. Its guidance is to keep cleaning up trails while the bait does its work; just keep soap and cleaners off the bait placement itself, as Kentucky warns.
**Seal the way in.** Caulk the cracks and openings the ants used. Kentucky singles out door thresholds, windows and the holes where utility pipes and wires enter the building.

**Fix what is feeding them outside.** Trim branches and shrubs so they do not touch the house (the Pacific Northwest guide suggests at least a foot of clearance) and deal with aphid-infested plants beside the walls.

body.text: A whole-house version of this plan, including what to do when the nest is inside a wall, is in [the guide to getting rid of ants in the house](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-ants-in-the-house).
Which bait works on sugar ants?

A slow-acting one. The University of California lists hydramethylnon, fipronil, boric acid and other borates, and abamectin as examples of bait active ingredients, and stresses that a bait must act slowly enough for foragers to make it back to the nest. The Pacific Northwest guide explains the mechanism: foragers store liquid food in a crop and regurgitate it to nestmates, which is how a slow-acting bait reaches ants that never leave the nest.

A weaker bait can do more. The University of California notes that prepackaged borate stations usually contain 5.4 percent borate, which can kill foragers before they bring the bait back to the colony, and that a liquid borate bait at a lower 0.5 to 1.0 percent in sugar water has more impact on the colony, although results may take several days to a week. The reasoning, and the limits of homemade mixes, are covered in [the guide to borax and boric acid ant baits](/blog/borax-for-ants). For product types, see [how bait stations differ from glue traps](/blog/best-ant-traps-canada) and [which kinds of ant killer reach the colony](/blog/best-ant-killer).
Why shouldn't you spray sugar ants?

Because spray kills the ants you can see and leaves the colony that sent them. The University of California states that spraying ants indoors will not stop more from coming in, and that treating around the foundation kills only foraging ants, typically a small proportion of the colony, without killing the queens. Spray also works against bait: the university tells readers not to use any insecticide spray while baiting, and Kentucky warns that insecticides or cleaners around a bait placement may deter ants from feeding.

There is a second concern with some of these species. Odorous house ants and pharaoh ants can keep many queens and spread by budding, in which part of a colony carries brood to a new site and starts another nest. The Pacific Northwest guide says budding may also occur when a colony is disturbed, and Kentucky describes odorous house ant nests as mobile, relocating fast and often in response to weather and disturbance. Texas A&M goes further: it says insecticide sprayed on ant trails kills only a few foraging workers and can sometimes make the problem worse by causing a colony to split into two or more separate colonies.

If you need the ants off the counter right now, use soap. The University of California says vacuuming a trail, or sponging or mopping it with soapy water, may be as effective as an insecticide spray at temporarily removing foragers. Many people reach for vinegar for the same job, and [what vinegar does and does not do to ants](/blog/does-vinegar-kill-ants) is covered separately. Keep any cleaner away from the bait itself.

body.title: Where the experts differ
body.text: Extension sources do not fully agree on outdoor sprays. Kentucky says a labeled liquid insecticide applied around the outside perimeter can reduce ant entry, while the University of California judges perimeter treatments less effective than a bait-based program and more likely to cause environmental problems.
How long does it take to get rid of sugar ants?

Expect days for the trail to thin and weeks for the colony. Kentucky says ant activity at a bait usually subsides in a few days as the colony declines. The University of California is more cautious: it can take 5 to 10 days to see fewer ants, and control with baits is not immediate and may take several weeks or more to be complete. Texas A&M's advice is to be patient, because it may take 3 to 4 weeks or more to eliminate some colonies. In the meantime, the University of California advises checking and refreshing bait stations regularly.

If the ants ignore a bait, change it. Kentucky describes ants as finicky feeders whose preferences can shift during the year, and advises trying another product when one is not attractive or does not seem to be working. For timing, the University of California notes that treatments made in late winter and early spring, when ant populations are just starting to grow, are the most effective.
Are sugar ants harmful?

Mostly they are a nuisance, not a hazard. The Pacific Northwest guide says odorous house ants do not sting and are ineffective biters, and that pavement ants can sting but rarely do. Texas A&M's table of house-infesting ants lists pharaoh ants, Argentine ants and little black ants as neither stinging nor biting, and the University of California adds that ants in general can bite with their jaws, although most species rarely do. The usual complaint is about food: the Washington State newsletter notes that ants indoors walk across food and may cause sanitation problems. Anyone who has a strong reaction to an insect bite or sting should contact a healthcare provider.

Large black ants are a different matter. The University of California describes carpenter ants as 1/4 to 1/2 inch long, nesting in places such as tree stumps, firewood, hollow doors and window frames and leaving sawdust-like frass outside the nest. If that sounds closer to what you are seeing, read about [carpenter ants and how their nests are found](/blog/carpenter-ants-canada) before you set out a sugar bait.
When should you call a professional for sugar ants?

Call one when bait, cleanup and sealing have not ended the trails after several weeks, or when the ants keep coming back. Kentucky's guide points householders to a professional when odorous house ants or other ants are a persistent problem, noting that pest control firms have more experience with ants and a broader range of insecticides and application equipment than the public. Texas A&M likewise says ant control can be difficult and that a commercial pest control operator is the next call if your own efforts do not succeed.

Pharaoh ants are the ones most likely to be nesting inside the building, since Texas A&M lists them as usually nesting indoors. The University of California places their nests in wall and cabinet voids and behind baseboards or insulation, and Texas A&M adds that their colonies multiply by budding, with a large part of the colony moving with some of its young to a new site. Reaching a colony inside wood or a wall void sometimes means drilling, and Texas A&M says that is a job for a professional with the skill and equipment to do it.

faqs.question: Are sugar ants and odorous house ants the same thing?
faqs.answer: Often, but not always. A Pacific Northwest Extension guide lists sugar ant as another name for the odorous house ant, along with stink ant and coconut ant, and a Washington State University newsletter says pavement ants get the name too. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension uses the same nickname for the pharaoh ant, a different species with different habits. Because the name moves from ant to ant, the reliable approach is to identify the insect itself. An odorous house ant is about 1/8 inch long, dark brown to black, and has a strong odor when crushed, while a pharaoh ant is about 1/16 inch long and yellow to light tan.

faqs.question: Do sugar ants bite or sting?
faqs.answer: Rarely. A Pacific Northwest Extension guide says odorous house ants do not sting and are ineffective biters, and that pavement ants can sting but rarely do. The University of California notes that ants in general can bite with their jaws, although most species rarely do. The small ants called sugar ants are mainly a nuisance around food. If you have a strong reaction to any insect bite or sting, contact a healthcare provider.

faqs.question: Why do I have sugar ants in a clean kitchen?
faqs.answer: Because crumbs are only one of the things they come for. The University of California says ants enter buildings seeking food and water, warmth and shelter, or refuge from hot, dry weather or flooding. A leaky faucet, a pet bowl or a film of grease can be enough. Some species also nest indoors: odorous house ants use wall and floor voids near warm, moist areas, and pharaoh ants nest in wall and cabinet voids. Outdoors, aphid-infested shrubs next to the house feed colonies that then send foragers inside.

faqs.question: What kills sugar ants instantly?
faqs.answer: Soapy water or a vacuum removes the ants you can see at once, and the University of California says this may be as effective as an insecticide spray for temporarily clearing foragers. It does nothing to the colony, though. The visible ants are a small portion of a nest that typically holds thousands more, including the queens. Ending the problem takes a slow-acting bait that workers carry home and share, which the university says can take 5 to 10 days to reduce numbers and several weeks or more to finish the job.

faqs.question: Where do sugar ants nest?
faqs.answer: It depends on the species. The University of Kentucky says odorous house ants commonly nest outdoors under mulch, stones, pavement, woodpiles, flower pots and siding, and indoors in wall cavities, appliances and potted plants. Pavement ants nest in lawns or under stones and boards, and Argentine ants nest outdoors in shallow mounds, according to the University of California. Pharaoh ants are the species Texas A&M lists as usually nesting indoors, in light sockets, potted plants, wall voids, attics and other cracks and crevices.

faqs.question: Will sugar ants go away on their own?
faqs.answer: A trail may disappear for a while, but you should not count on the colony leaving. The University of Kentucky describes odorous house ant nests as mobile, relocating quickly when the weather changes or the nest is disturbed, so ants can vanish from one room and turn up in another. A Pacific Northwest Extension guide adds that colonies nesting indoors stay active all year. Removing food and water reduces activity, but while the nest and its queens survive, foragers can return, which is why baiting the colony is the recommended fix.
